summary: Extends SDP with two bandwidth modifiers that state how much bandwidth is allowed for RTCP packets in an RTP session. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Video calls send control reports in the background as well as the picture. This memo adds a way to say how much room those reports can use.

questions: what are sdp rs and rr modifiers
how much bandwidth does rtcp use
how to turn off rtcp receiver reports
subtitle: Two SDP bandwidth modifiers, RS and RR, that set how much bandwidth RTCP may use.

tldr.problem: RTCP normally gets 5% of the session bandwidth, but some applications need an RTCP budget that is set independently of the data rate, or that differs for senders and receivers.
tldr.mechanism: SDP gains two bandwidth modifiers, b=RS for active data senders and b=RR for other participants, both in bits per second.
tldr.outcome: Session descriptions can now state RTCP bandwidth directly, including turning off receiver reports by setting RR to zero. Large values can cause denial of service, so receivers should validate them.

today: RFC 3556 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the RS and RR modifiers registered in the SDP "bwtype" table.

sections.title: Why Set RTCP Bandwidth Separately
sections.content:
RTP (RFC 3550) comes with a control protocol, RTCP, that carries synchronization information from data senders and feedback from receivers. Normally RTCP is allocated 5% of the session bandwidth.

The RFC gives reasons to decouple the two. A rate-adaptive application may adapt its data rate downward while the session bandwidth stays at the maximum, so a separate RTCP figure lets RTCP stay under 5% of the actual data bandwidth. In the other direction, an application that sends data at a very low rate but wants to send extra RTCP such as APP packets may need more than 5%.

An RTP profile may also split RTCP bandwidth between active data senders and everyone else. Setting the non-sender share to zero turns off reception reports while senders can still send sender reports for inter-media synchronization. The RFC does not recommend turning off reception reports, because they are needed for reception quality feedback and congestion control. It says doing so may suit unidirectional links or sessions with other ways to avoid congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the status notes get a small fixed slice of the call's room. Sometimes that slice is too big or too small, so this memo lets you pick the size yourself.

sections.title: The RS and RR Modifiers
sections.content:
SDP has an optional bandwidth line, b=<modifier>:<bandwidth-value>, where the default unit is kilobits per second. A typical modifier is AS, the application specific maximum for one media stream from one site.

This memo adds two modifiers: b=RS:<bandwidth-value> is the RTCP bandwidth for active data senders, and b=RR:<bandwidth-value> is the RTCP bandwidth for other participants (receivers). The allocation covers all RTCP packet types, including SR, RR, SDES, BYE, APP and any future types.

Unlike other SDP bandwidth modifiers, the value for these two is an integer number of bits per second, because the desired RTCP bandwidth may be less than 1 kb/s. The RFC notes this conflicts with the original SDP specification (RFC 2327). At the 44th IETF meeting two fixes were considered, fractional values or different units, and the second was preferred so the syntax stays unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two new labels you can write in a call description: one for how much room the speakers' notes get and one for the listeners' notes. They are counted in small units so tiny amounts are possible.

sections.title: How the Split Behaves
sections.content:
The exact effect depends on the algorithm a given RTP profile uses to compute the RTCP reporting interval. For the RTP A/V Profile (RFC 3551), which uses the default algorithm in RFC 3550, at least RS/(RS+RR) of the RTCP bandwidth goes to active senders. If the share of senders among participants is at or below that ratio, each sender gets RS divided by the number of senders. If senders are a larger share, they get their proportion of the sum, so a sender and a non-sender each get the same allocation. It is therefore not possible to limit senders to less RTCP bandwidth than non-senders.

Special cases:

  • If RR is zero, non-senders never get any RTCP bandwidth, however many senders there are.
  • If RS is zero, senders can still send RTCP, but are treated like non-senders.
  • If both are zero, calculating RS/(RS+RR) would be unwise.
sections.plainLanguage: Speakers get at least their set share of the note room. If there are many speakers, they share more of it, but a speaker never gets less than a listener.

sections.title: Defaults and Precedence
sections.content:
If RS or RR is omitted, the RTP profile in use supplies the default. For the Audio/Video Profile, total RTCP bandwidth is 5% of the session bandwidth. If one specifier is omitted, its value is 5% minus the other, but not less than zero. If both are omitted, sender and receiver RTCP get 1.25% and 3.75% of the session bandwidth. The memo sets no limits on values other than that they must be non-negative, though the RTP specification and profile may.

Bandwidth lines may appear at session level (shared by all media), at media level (for one medium), or both. From highest to lowest precedence:

  1. Explicit RR or RS at media level
  2. Explicit RR or RS at session level
  3. Default based on the session bandwidth specifier at media level
  4. Default based on the session bandwidth specifier at session level

One consequence is that setting RR to zero at session level turns off RTCP for non-data-senders in all media.
sections.plainLanguage: If you write a rule for one part of the call, it wins over a rule for the whole call, and a written rule always wins over the built-in guess.

sections.title: An Example
sections.content: The RFC's example SDP description has an audio medium with b=AS:64, b=RS:800 and b=RR:2400, and a video medium with b=AS:256, b=RS:800 and b=RR:2400. For audio, the explicit values equal the defaults and could be omitted. For video, the RTCP bandwidths are set for a data bandwidth of 64 kb/s even though the maximum is 256 kb/s, on the assumption that video will adapt to a lower rate under network conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: The video can use up to a lot of room, but the call expects to use less, so the status-note room is sized for the smaller amount.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The SDP specification (RFC 2327) requires new bandwidth modifiers to be registered with IANA by reference to a standards-track RFC that gives precise semantics, says when to use them, and explains why existing modifiers do not suffice. This document is intended to meet those requirements. The names RS and RR have been registered in the "bwtype" table of the SDP Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The two new labels were written in an official list so nobody else uses the same names for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of SDP apply to descriptions containing these modifiers. In addition, a bandwidth value could be unreasonably large and make an application send RTCP at an excessive rate, causing denial of service. This is like the risk of an unreasonable media bandwidth, though encoders usually have a limited range.

Applications should validity-check all parameters received in an SDP description, especially one that is not authenticated. The memo cannot set limits because they depend on the RTP profile and application.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone writes a huge number, a program might flood the line with notes. So programs should check numbers before trusting them.
